title: AI is mass decompiling games. That's both awesome and scary.
raw_summary: AI is mass decompiling games. That's both awesome and scary. Indie game developer Popcar talks about the recent wave of AI-powered decompilation of existing games, enabling weird mashups between existing games, and producing a boom in game preservation projects to get old games working on new hardware (often in a browser using WebAssembly). I like how this piece captures both the positives and the negatives of this new development: Most people already realized the scary part by now. If AI can decompile games and software, then the entire tech industry is about to explode. Anybody can decompile other software and use it any way they'd like, and nobody can stop them. Companies can steal from competitors. Your paid game or app can be open-sourced against your will. This isn't exclusive to old video games, we can apply this to any software. [...] This is also a big win for preservation. Old games can be ported, modified, enhanced, and made much more easily accessible than before. [...[ With console makers going all in on digital and games becoming entirely unplayable due to servers shutting down, this is fantastic news. title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
raw_summary: Redesigning source control at Anthropic Interesting piece from Anthropic describing why and how they built their own custom alternative to Git, based on the dramatic increase in rate of changes to their code after the past six months. In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. They included a chart showing those changes. I had Claude modify their chart ( code here ) to add markers for the public releases of each of their models in 2026: This shows public release dates, not the date when models became available for Anthropic's internal use. My guess is that the introduction of Fable/Mythos class models is a key factor in the increased coding velocity. "Antique" is their new code review system. The source control system is called Scion, and sounds to me like a reinvention of centralized source control along the lines of Subversion. They had some pretty extreme requirements: The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day. The new system was built by a team of seven people, and the migration from Git was completed in five months. When asked on Hacker News about the lack of offline support, Scion engineer Nick G replied : Since Claude is by far the heaviest user of Scion and is necessarily online, this just wasn't important to do. As an aside, I've been trying adversarial review in my own projects recently, where you have a model try and find flaws (I often play Claude and GPT off against each other). This note from the article reflected my own experience with that: Anthropic also makes extensive use of adversarial review, and, while this is incredibly effective in many ways, it can also be myopic, so skilled engineers needed to steer Claude away from over-engineering parts of the system in response to hypothetical concerns. Via Hacker News Tags: git , migrations , version-control , ai , generative-ai , llms , anthropic , agentic-engineering

title: Hello Python 3.15, goodbye 3.10, and now I can use 3.11
raw_summary: Python 3.15 is here ! Here's the essential What's new in Python 3.15 guide, this year curated by 3.14 and 3.15 release manager Hugo van Kemenade. As someone who builds open source software that works in every supported Python version, I get to say goodbye to Python 3.10 and start embracing features from Python 3.11. First, some highlights from Python 3.15. Explicit lazy imports I'm most excited about Explicit lazy imports from PEP 810 . These let you import modules like so: lazy import json lazy from pathlib import Path The module will then be imported the first time those symbols are used in the code that follows. My LLM CLI tool implements plugins. I had to recommend manual lazy imports in the plugin author documentation, because simply installing plugins that used heavy dependencies such as sentence_transformers could add multiple seconds to every invocation of the llm command. Lazy imports directly address this startup cost. Unpacking in comprehensions The new [*sublist for sublist in lists] unpacking syntax is neat. Here's an illustration lifted from the documentation : lists = [[ 1 , 2 ], [ 3 , 4 ], [ 5 ]] [ * L for L in lists ] # [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] # equivalent to [x for L in lists for x in L] sets = [{ 1 , 2 }, { 2 , 3 }, { 3 , 4 }] { * s for s in sets } # {1, 2, 3, 4} # equivalent to {x for s in sets for x in s} dicts = [{ 'a' : 1 }, { 'b' : 2 }, { 'a' : 3 }] { ** d for d in dicts } # {'a': 3, 'b': 2} # equivalent to {k: v for d in dicts for k,v in d.items()} PEP 798: Unpacking in Comprehensions by Adam Hartz and Erik Demaine proposed this as an extension of the unpacking syntax from PEP 448 , which landed in Python 3.5 back in 2015. A sampling profiler Python's existing tracing profiler has been renamed from cProfile to profiling.tracing , and has been joined by an exciting new sampling profiler called Tachyon, aka profiling.sampling . Sampling profilers work by periodically capturing stack traces from running processes, then using those to calculate which functions have the most time spent inside of them. They're very low overhead and can provide a deep insight into running systems, without needing to instrument those systems first. I've previously used tools like py-spy for this. Now this capability is baked into the standard library. If you have the PID of an existing Python 3.15 process you can start gathering samples by running this (I had to use sudo on macOS): sudo uv run --python 3.15 python -m profiling.sampling attach 1234 Interact with the main program a bit, then hit Ctrl+C to stop gathering and see a report, which looks something like this: It can also produce flame graphs like this and heat maps like this , and can even output a format that can be viewed in the Firefox profiler UI. 3.15 isn't much faster than 3.14 Miguel Grinberg investigated How fast is Python 3.15? the other day against the 3.15.0rc3 release and found performance to be mostly the same as 3.14, with the exception of the experimental JIT. The JIT gave a 1.2x boost over the standard 3.15 interpreter (on a Fibonacci test), the first time Miguel observed a meaningful JIT performance increase. Miguel's explorations of 3.14 last year found significant boosts against Python 3.13 across many more categories. Upgrading to Python 3.15 with uv I used the following sequence of commands to get uv to use Python 3.15 on my Mac. First I had to upgrade uv itself to ensure it knew about the new release: uv self update Then I installed the stable 3.15 release: uv python install 3.15 And told uv that I wanted that to be the default for every uv run command, unless the project itself pinned a different version: uv python pin --global 3.15 Now the following reports 3.15 as the version: uv run python --version I already have a bunch of tools installed using uv tool install . I reinstalled them to use Python 3.15 like this: uv tool upgrade datasette --python 3.15 Then I can confirm the version like this: datasette --get /-/versions.json | jq Highlights from Python 3.11 The release of 3.15 means that Python 3.10 (released in 2021) is officially no longer supported . My policy for my main open source projects is to keep them working in every supported Python version. I can now drop 3.10 and start using features that were introduced in 3.11. Here's the What's new in Python 3.11 document. I finally get to rely on tomllib being available! Datasette makes extensive use of asyncio . 3.11 adds TaskGroup and timeout() , and several more new features. datetime.UTC is a new in 3.11 alias for datetime.timezone.utc . Python's SQLite support got some significant upgrades in 3.11, including: setlimit() and getlimit() expose a mechanism for setting SQLite runtime limits from Python. create_window_function() lets us create custom window functions in Python, as a class with step() , value() , inverse() , and finalize() methods. blobopen() provides an efficient mechanism for partial reads and writes of large BLOB binary values stored in a SQLite row. You can now call set_authorizer(None) to remove a SQLite authorizer. Datasette had a workaround for this! Plus a whole bunch of improvements to Python's typing system . I plan to land Python 3.11 improvements to a bunch of my projects over the next few weeks. Here's my first Datasette PR removing that set_authorizer(None) workaround. title: Deno is joining Cloudflare
raw_summary: Deno is joining Cloudflare The Deno team released the first version of celld back in August - their open source implementation of the Durable Objects pattern from Cloudflare Workers. Today, Cloudflare are acquiring Deno outright, with the goal of building on celld to "make workerd self-hosting a first-class supported way to build and run apps using the Workers programming model" (see the Cloudflare blog .) The bad news is that Deno itself will not be maintained by Cloudflare beyond the next year: We will support the Deno runtime for another year with monthly releases containing bug fixes and security updates. After that year we will end our development of the Deno runtime. Deno will remain open source, and we welcome others who want to continue its development. Deno (and Node.js) creator Ryan Dahl explained that decision in a comment on Hacker News: It's a joint decision and I agree with it. I'm most invested in its success and have put the most work into it - and I no longer think it's where I can do the most important work. There are some good ideas in Deno and it's well engineered - but it ultimately is not solving big problems. It has been sucked into the gravity well of node compatibility, which forces it to behave exactly as Node does. Why reimplement Node? It works. Marginal performance or UX or security benefits are not enough. I'm interested in building powerful new abstractions. celld has been working remarkably well, depending only on object storage for coordination and persistence. It is not just a slightly different API to interact with the file system or network - it's an entirely new model for server development. My favorite feature of Deno has long been the permissions system, where you can run a Deno script and specify exactly which files and folders it can read and write to, and which network hosts it can access. Node.js has a similar permissions model these days, added in Node v20.0.0 in April 2023 and declared stable in Node v22.13.0 in January 2025. They don't yet support allow-listing specific network hosts though - networking is either on or off. Via Hacker News Tags: cloudfront , javascript , nodejs , ryan-dahl , sandboxing , deno

title: A new feature for my blog, built using my voice
raw_summary: I shipped a new feature for my blog today: the Newsletters page, which offers an index of all of the newsletters I've sent out, both my free weekly Substack and my monthly sponsors-only updates. I built the feature almost entirely using my voice, chatting away to my laptop while I cooked dinner. Codex voice mode I used the ChatGPT desktop app for this, in the Codex tab, using the voice conversation mode, running against a local development environment. Here's what that looks like: I started the session against my local simonwillisonblog checkout by typing: Start dev server and open in browser This gave me a preview of the site that it would be working on, and meant that I could later ask it to show me the new pages so I could visually track its progress. Then I clicked the "Start new voice chat" button - that's not the microphone button, it's the one to the right of it - and set my laptop up in the kitchen so I could talk to it while I cooked. Talking to my computer I had a pretty good idea of what I wanted to build, and it's a simple enough Django feature that I was certain the model (in this case GPT-6 Astra High) would be able to do it. A new model, a migration, some view code, templates, and a couple of import functions to populate the database from external sources. Here's an extract of my voice transcript that was captured by Codex: Um, they do not. Um, this is going to be a new type of content. Um, it's not going to show up... Oh, hold on. Yeah, no- I do not want this to show up in my, um, tag pages and date archive pages and... Actually, no, I think... I don't want it on the tag pages. I don't want it on the, um, blog index page. But I think I do want it to show up on the date-based pages. You know, if you navigate to September the 19th, and I sent a newsletter on that page, I think I want that to show up. So... this is- so I think we probably need a new model. The other thing is that I want them searchable, uh the Substack ones are not searchable, because those are actually just copies of other s- on content on my blog. These monthly ones do contain unique content, and spe- and once they're... published, like once they're made public a month after they've gone out, I want them to show up on my search results. Apparently this was clear enough that the model knew what I wanted to build! You can read the full transcript, disfluencies and all, in this Gist . We went on like this for about half an hour (the time it took to cook dinner). The model would reply and occasionally ask clarifying questions, then get to work modifying the code. What we built We got a surprisingly long way entirely by voice: A new model and migration to represent imported newsletters in Django, plus Django Admin configuration for that Four working imports: The most recent Substack items via RSS Every other Substack item via their undocumented API, which GPT-6 Astra knew about (it tried /api/v1/archive directly) and then ran a search to figure out how to paginate it and found this article by Karen Spinner All of my published monthly newsletters from my simonw/monthly-newsletter-archive GitHub repository My most recent private sponsors-only newsletter from a private repository The /newsletters/ and /newsletters/2026/ public archive pages Newsletters showing up on day and month archive pages too, but not on tag pages or my homepage Weekly Substack newsletters link to Substack; archived monthly newsletters have their own pages Integration with my site search engine It was almost ready to ship. The catch was the imports: Astra offered to export data from my local copy so I could import that into production, but I wanted it to work like my other import scripts. Since some of the data lived in a private GitHub repository, this would involve creating a new API key, and for that I knew I'd have to sit at the keyboard for a while. Finishing it with a review Once I had finished cooking and judged it mostly feature-complete, I had Codex create a branch and open a pull request. I reviewed the code in the GitHub PR interface. It was nearly what I needed, except it had chosen to use Git in a subprocess for one of the import scripts. I needed one of the imports to pull from a private Git repository, so I figured the API would be a better bet. I switched to typing and had Codex swap that out for an API-based import instead. You can see the changes I made during the review in the extra commits on the PR . I fixed the import mechanism and made a few tweaks to the display of those public pages. It took an additional half hour of typing-based prompting to get to the point where I was happy to deploy it to production by landing the PR. The end result You can see the end result at the new newsletters index page , or view the page for a previous monthly newsletter . The index page shows my most recent Substack weekly newsletters and GitHub sponsors monthly newsletters mixed together in reverse chronological order. Further down the page are links to my by-year archive pages. GPT-6 Astra designed the page, and then tweaked that design based on my vocal feedback from glancing at the local preview across the kitchen. Better for multi-tasking than as a daily driver OpenAI love using voice-driven demos like this one for things like DevDay - and they do work well in that environment. I don't think this is going to be a daily driver for me though. I've written before about how much "work" I get done using ChatGPT voice mode on my phone while walking the dog - mostly research and brainstorming, but occasionally actual development work by having ChatGPT write and test out snippets of code. This feels different. The addition of the visual preview, plus being able to type or paste things in via the keyboard when I need to communicate something that doesn't work vocally, makes this a much more powerful way of interacting with a coding agent. I still switch back to typing once I get down to the details of things though. Being able to paste in examples and error messages, or directly highlight the code or feature that needs changing, remains more efficient than trying to describe it in words. I mainly work from home, which is good because there's no way I'd want to talk to my computer like this in a shared workspace! The killer feature for me is the ability to multi-task. I usually cook with a podcast or TikTok running; now I can actually build stuff instead. It came out almost a year ago , and was priced at $1/million input and $5/million output - relatively expensive even back then, and a full 10x the price of OpenAI's GPT-6 Luna , released last month. title: Search and Increasing Returns, or, No One Makes You Push to Github
raw_summary: Attention conservation notice : An economistic argument that computer networks are nigh-doomed to effective centralization, by someone who is neither an economist nor a computer scientist. Arcane, speculative, and not actionable even if correct. You would be better off spending your time reading a book . Drafted in 2018, and deliberately not much updated. Posted now because I found myself re-using the joke of the subtitle in an e-mail. Twitter is awful for many reasons , but not the least of them is the way it makes its users feel forced to keep using it. ( One such complaint among many .) Early visions of how it could contribute to a beneficient or at least harmless ecosystem, such Steven Berlin Johnson's (*), presumed that it would be much less sticky , a more old-fashioned website people could leave. Now, more recently Johnson has written a spectacularly wrong-headed piece hailing blockchain as a blow for re-decentralizing the Web. Of course, the primary working example of a block chain is Bitcoin, which is heavily centralized in holdings, in processing power, and in exchanges. And there are economies-of-scale reasons to expect this would be true of anything using either proof of work or proof of stake. But suppose the problem with Bitcoin is just that it's not got a very compelling use: imagine if keeping your car idling 24/7 produced solved Sudokus you could trade for heroin --- @Theophite, 16 August 2018 and that nobody has a use for blockchains , not really. Git repositories, on the other hand, are the part of the blockchain idea that's actually good for something: a way of tracking changes, with many authors, where it is very, very hard to go back and alter history without being caught. And git repositories are things that are in-principle easy to copy and move around, and could be hosted on any machine running HTTP (or, heck, FTP). So why does Github exist , let alone hold the position it does? The answer, I think, comes in two parts. The first is that focal points are subject to increasing returns via network effects. The second is that search engines create and/or amplify focal points . Put these two together, and you get a very strong tendency for any particular line of activity --- be it trading solved sudokus for heroin or open-source software development --- to concentrate in just one, or at most a few, online locations. Incidentally: This doesn't necessarily lock in first-mover advantage, because other forces can overcome this (revulsion, technical superiority), but it does mean that it will be very hard to avoid having at most a few dominant locations at any one time. It also means that the transitions between dominant locations will be brief . If we really wanted to re-decentralize, we'd have to (1) get rid of focal points, or (2) get rid of search engines as we've known them, or (3) somehow make search conduct users to a distributed, decentralized focal "non-point" (focal blob? focal rhizome?). I therefore strongly suspect we are not going to re-decentralize. But then I didn't expect the Web would centralize as much as it has, despite having literally learned my Brian Arthur and Paul David at my father's knee, so what do I know? *: To be clear, I have been a fan of Johnson's books since Interface Culture and Emergence . I am picking on two of his essays, but that's because I think he is too ready to find encouraging signs for a certain vision of how the Internet could transform the world for the better. To be clear, I share the vision, but now hold out little hope for it . (Tweakage, 2 June 2026: Small changes in the last paragraph, avoid re-using the word "point" so much.) title: What changes when your design system can talk to an AI?
raw_summary: Rebuilding a UI with QuantumBlack Design System, Claude Code, and the Figma MCP In our recent blog post, “ When everyone can build, design is the differentiator ”, we introduced QuantumBlack Design System (QBDS). We made the argument that an AI-native design system is more than a component library and its purpose is as an infrastructure that lets agentic developers make fewer guesses. The article described the system and our philosophy. Over the past few weeks, we have re-platformed the entire UI of one of our products onto QBDS, one that previously had a production dashboard built on an older shadcn layout that predated QBDS. In numbers, it runs to 21 pages, 13 modals, 40 UI primitives and somewhere around 96 supporting components. A refactor of this size used to mean months of redlines and handoff documents. We’ll describe what we discovered from using QBDS, both from the engineering side and the design side. In this post we’ll describe what happened when we put QuantumBlack Design System to work. The setup We used a small stack since QBDS supplies the components, the tokens, and the agent guidance described in the earlier QBDS article linked above. We used Figma to hold the target designs, and Claude Code for the implementation, connected through the Figma MCP server . We crafted an internal QuantumBlack front-end developer skill to package QBDS guidance in the form an agent can act on. That skill lives on Brix , our inner source platform for sharing artefacts. The workflow Our front-end engineer runs a page migration roughly as shown in the diagram. A typical page migration workflow for a FE engineer. Spin up the app locally with hot reloading. Give Claude the context: the PR, a screenshot of the current screen, the target Figma node, and the skill. Instruct the agent to ask when something isn’t trivial. Review every change as it lands live, through hot reload. Run unit tests and lint (Claude fixes most failures itself), then draft the PR, run CI/CD, and run manual Playwright E2E tests on a local minikube. Use a review bot initially, then have a human review the result before the merge. Step 3 is more than a throwaway. For example, when Claude migrated the Secrets page, the Figma node left two questions open: how row actions should render, and what to do with two modals the design didn’t cover. Rather than making a guess, it set out the gaps, weighed each option against the pages we’d already migrated, and asked for clarification. We answered in two lines and it then completed the build. The agent noticed that one option “diverges from other migrated tables,” which means that the agent had to know what the other migrated tables do. This knowledge came about because QBDS encodes patterns and relationships, not only components, which is the benefit of using QBDS over a plain component library. In time terms: a simple table page with an existing sibling pattern took 10 to 15 minutes end to end, with tests and build included. A complex screen from scratch took 4 to 5 hours. If we had worked on this migration by hand, both would have taken days. What the design side measures Our designer’s comparison is against a similar product we shipped last year, before QBDS or any of this tooling existed: First-pass fidelity to Figma: around 20 percent previously, 70–80 percent now we’re using this workflow. Review rounds per screen: four or more previously, and the result often still wasn’t right. One or two now, and the result is correct. Component reuse: we now reuse about 90 percent from stock QBDS components. The other 10 percent is custom, but assembled from QBDS micro-elements as a starting point. QA and handoff: three-plus hours per screen previously, much of it spent writing Figma documentation so engineering could interpret intent, and we sometimes also needed a meeting to decide. With the new workflow we now need twenty minutes to an hour. This is a key result because previously handoff was a translation problem from human to agent. Now we can use QBDS, the system documentation is already readable by the agent, so most of the laborious translation work is now unnecessary. A typical page before and after refactoring. The broader role of a designer It’s difficult to capture this in a metric, but ultimately, designers on our team don’t live in Figma any more. We’ve expanded our AI skills and ways of working, so depending on what we’re trying to solve, that might mean working in Figma, Cursor, or Claude Code, or moving between them. The choice of tool becomes more intentional, based on what each part of the problem actually needs. With QBDS in the codebase, we can work against the same system the product actually ships with. Through the Figma MCP, our QBDS skills and Code Connect, we carry context between design and code instead of recreating it at every step. When something is easier to explore visually, we work in Figma. When we want to experience it in the real product, we move into code. That changes the traditional design-to-development handoff. With AI, designers can take an idea further, from exploring the experience to composing it with real components, implementing the front end, and experiencing the design in the actual product. AI doesn’t get everything right by default, and the quality of the result depends heavily on the context and tools we give the agent. Explicitly calling the relevant QBDS skill and verifying that the agent is using the MCP correctly can make the difference between something that only looks close and something that follows the design system. The difference became clear when we ran the same task twice: recreating the product experience in Figma with an agent. In the first attempt we didn’t explicitly call our QBDS skill. In the second, we called the skill and verified the MCP usage. The improvement in component usage, icons, styles and overall fidelity was immediately apparent. The full prompt sequence behind this exercise is in our prompt playbook. Comparing the upper images where the agent didn’t use a QBDS skill with the lower images which called the skill and verified MCP usage. Note the significant improvement, particularly to the workflow studio page. The new design flow The workflow is much more flexible for us as we can move between design and code depending on the requirements. 0. Feature request. The starting point varies. A product manager might create a ticket, a designer might identify an opportunity, or a developer might already have a working draft that needs UX refinement. 1. Ideation and prototyping. We move between the Figma MCP, QBDS skills, QBDS Code Connect, Cursor, Claude Code and Vercel. Ideas can start directly with AI and quickly become working prototypes. When something is too complex for the AI to resolve well, we design it in Figma and bring that context back into code through the MCP. With Vercel, we can also create shareable versions early and test ideas with stakeholders before treating them as finished. 2. Code to Figma, and design refinement. Sometimes the working prototype becomes the starting point for deeper design refinement. We bring it back into Figma, where we can work with more precision on the parts that need it, while keeping the experience connected to the same design system. 3. The new design handoff. The handoff is no longer necessarily a finished set of screens in Figma. Depending on the feature, we might keep the key components in Figma while handing over a working prototype in a dedicated repository or branch. A typical new design workflow. Figma remains important for giving designers visibility and control over the components we already have, and a place to explore specific design changes. The working implementation carries those decisions closer to the actual product. Engineering then brings the deeper code expertise to validate the implementation, and make sure what ultimately ships is robust and production-ready. title: Solving the data lineage problem that’s holding enterprise AI back
raw_summary: AI4Data by QuantumBlack, AI by McKinsey Data estates rarely become complex by design. They grow through acquisitions, new platforms, local workarounds, and repeated efforts to connect, consolidate, or retire legacy systems. While such changes are often necessary, each one opens the door to duplicated data, undocumented transformation logic, and inconsistent definitions. Even when individual datasets are high quality, teams may no longer know the lineage of data, that is, where a value originated, nor how it changed between systems, or which version should be treated as authoritative. Most enterprises still build lineage manually. Teams piece it together from institutional knowledge, often relying on the few subject-matter experts who remember how a dataset was assembled. Because documentation is frequently incomplete and becomes outdated quickly, analysts spend disproportionate time finding and validating data. Projects are stalled, data is duplicated rather than reused, and different teams repeatedly investigate the same relationships. This article describes how to accelerate the creation of trusted, end-to-end data lineage. Everyone has a reason to invest in data lineage Until recently, the firms that invested seriously in lineage were regulated firms such as banks, insurers, and healthcare organizations, and they did it because their regulators required it. Since 2020, those sectors have paid more than $1.4B in finalized regulatory penalties, often due to deficient monitoring and reporting frameworks, and failures to meet standards such as BCBS 239. The response was to throw people at the problem. In complex data environments, tracing the path of a single element from report to data source can take weeks, largely because the relevant knowledge is scattered across ETL tools, data catalogs, and the memories of individual employees. Firms outside regulated industries looked at that cost and reasonably decided they could live without lineage. Unresolved lineage stands in the way of both regulatory compliance and the cost reductions that come from a modernized legacy data estate. The scale of the underlying spend explains why: procuring data sources and maintaining data governance can account for roughly a fifth of total IT spend at a large institution, with more than half of that going toward data controls and manual governance activity alone. By improving lineage and reducing the effort required to trace, validate, and remediate data issues, organizations may be able to realize an estimated $30–100M in cost savings. The harder-won benefit is trust: executives get a defensible reason to believe the dashboards they already use and the agents they are being asked to rely on. An AI agent asked to answer a question from enterprise data has to know which source is authoritative and what happened to a value between systems. Without lineage, the agent either guesses or the organization refuses to trust what it returns. Every sector deploying agents now needs lineage across a far wider slice of the estate than a regulatory report ever covered. Manual lineage can’t keep pace Most lineage tools available today are point solutions which trace how data moves within a single system, leaving organizations struggling when faced with more complex enterprise estates. It’s not unusual for an estate to comprise dozens of systems, built years or decades apart, on a wide variety of legacy platforms and programming languages with undocumented logic. This helps explain why up to three-quarters of organizations still rely on manual work to trace the lineage of their most critical data, an incredibly slow and expensive process. Manually tracing a single data element end-to-end across legacy and cloud systems typically has a direct cost of one to three million dollars. Recent advancements in AI that have emerged over the past year enable the interpretation of code and metadata alongside the raw data itself, detecting connections across any environment or platform. These automated tools can complement the lineage tools organizations already have, closing gaps between them and accelerating those tasks that used to require an army of analysts. This rest of this article explains how AI for data lineage (AI4DL) from QuantumBlack, AI by McKinsey, addresses a shared bottleneck by accelerating lineage creation, to give organizations a clearer view of where data comes from and how it changes across systems. AI4DL accelerates one core task across four common use cases AI4DL is an accelerator that combines AI-based detection methods with human validation to identify complete, end-to-end lineage across whatever mix of systems and technologies a client happens to run. It’s designed to capture lineage faster and more completely, engendering greater trust than any manual approach can. AI4DL is an accelerator for creating lineage output that is reusable, and provides many different types of business value, depending on the use case. Regulatory traceability: AI4DL gives compliance teams real and up-to-date visibility into how data flows, transforms, and depends on other data across systems. Improved data and business understanding: AI4DL exposes origins, dependencies, transformations, and consumption patterns across the data estate. Migration readiness: AI4DL accelerates the mapping between legacy and modern data models, cutting the effort required for platform and code migrations. AI and analytics implementation: AI4DL gives AI agents validated context for finding, interpreting, and using enterprise data. Together, these benefits build a level of trust that enables a regulator, a migration lead, and a data engineering team to point to the same underlying lineage graph and trust it for their own purposes, rather than maintaining separate, often incomplete versions of the truth. Solving data lineage can unlock gen Al and agentic workflows in organizations. Productivity is the shared economic benefit across all four use cases. By reducing manual lineage documentation, investigation, and validation, AI4DL frees data, engineering, governance, and subject-matter experts to focus on higher-value work. AI detection and human checks AI4DL works by running various detection methods in parallel, each tuned to a different signal in the data estate: LLM-based metadata inference reads data catalogs (table and column names, descriptions, constraints, tags, owners) to infer likely lineage. LLM-based code review parses ETL and ELT code, from SQL to PySpark to DAGs, to derive column-level lineage and summarize what each transformation actually does. Statistical attribute matching suggests column similarities between different datasets using data profiling and distribution similarity. The same approach used for a single COBOL program, for example, can be scaled to two thousand or more, with the same degree of accuracy and trust. Whatever combination of methods applies, the results are never taken at face value. The tool flags low confidence decisions and human experts review the resulting lineage graphs, so that they flag inconsistencies before anything is treated as fact. This human check is what allows AI4DL’s output to be treated as audit-grade rather than merely directional, a critical distinction in regulated industries. The results Example: A major Latin American bank pursuing an AI-first strategy was being held back by data quality issues with ten years of real-time credit card and investment data, more than 34 billion rows spread across 2,000-plus COBOL programs and 50-plus DB2 tables. By decomposing that metadata and code into end-to-end lineage and layering AI models on top, the bank cut lineage creation time from ten weeks to a few hours, freeing roughly 50,000 combined hours for its data governance and engineering teams. title: When everyone can build, design is the differentiator
raw_summary: An open-source project from QuantumBlack, AI by McKinsey Here at QuantumBlack , we’ve had an internal design system for a while. It’s powered multiple products and gives our development teams a consistent language to help them ship faster. But it was built for a different era. The original architecture worked well for designers and developers, but it wasn’t set up for AI-assisted development. Now we’ve rebuilt it to make it easier for both human team members and AI agents to use, customize, and extend. We are sharing part of the new design system infrastructure as an open-source project , giving our clients and other external teams a practical way to adopt it in their own products. The previous design system held components, design tokens and documentation. QuantumBlack Design System rebuilds those and adds a design-code link, guidelines, design intent, agent skills and project context. In this article, we explain what makes a design system AI-native, share what we learned rebuilding ours on shadcn and Tailwind, and describe where we think design infrastructure goes next. Our belief: the design system is where design scales AI makes interface implementation faster and more widely available. That puts more weight on decisions generation alone cannot make: whether an interface works, whether it is appropriate for its users, and whether it should be built at all. Good judgment, critical design thinking, taste, and trust have become more important than ever. If design is the differentiator, then a design system is the way to scale it. In the past, design systems were mainly component libraries that kept products consistent. Today they’re more fundamental as a shared infrastructure that captures an organization’s design intelligence and makes it available to every product, every team, and, increasingly, every AI tool. The best design systems enforce consistency and help humans and AI build better products and solutions together. Unlike most design systems, ours isn’t built for a single product or company. We deploy design and code across a variety of McKinsey clients, industries, and brands, which means our system has to scale. It has to capture design decisions, foundations, principles, guidelines, structure, and intent that work in different contexts. QuantumBlack Design System supports agentic workflows, product building, prototypes and POCs, consistency at scale, a replicable playbook, client ecosystems, brand theming, and design-code handoff. We’ve spent years on the closely related design problem of explaining AI/ML reasoning to people so they trust it. Building an AI-native design system reverses that challenge, so that we are now teaching AI to understand and apply human design judgment. Design infrastructure, not a component library An AI-native design system is more than a collection of components; it includes the infrastructure that helps AI build the right thing. That means going beyond reusable UI to defining a system that encodes design values and the intent behind them. Every component, token, guideline, and connection between design and code must be explicit. The less AI has to guess, the more consistent, explainable, and production-ready its output becomes. A clean, well-structured, well-documented design system is now one of the highest-value investments a design team can make, because every AI tool in the organization inherits its quality…or its mess. This benefits people too. The process of making a system understandable to AI forces greater clarity between designers and engineers, creating a shared source of truth that everyone can build from. That clarity serves the AI as well as every human designer and engineer who has to understand the system, not to mention every user who consumes its outputs. Good structure also makes AI more efficient and cost-effective. Better structure means fewer iterations, fewer unnecessary tokens, improved output accuracy and consistency, and overall lower cost to reach a production-ready result. We designed for this deliberately, down to letting the system steer work toward the correct technical path for the job, rather than defaulting to a heavier setup that the task may not require. Better structure means fewer rounds to reach production. QuantumBlack Design System brings together design tokens, components, documentation, and agent skills into a single foundation. The more knowledge it captures, the better every product and every AI workflow built on top of it becomes. It is executable knowledge, not just documentation. Agents can learn the principles and use the implementation directly, turning design guidance into something they can both reference and reason with. We treat agent guidance as part of the design system. Alongside design tokens and components, we package the project context, implementation guidance, and reusable capabilities that help agents navigate the system consistently. Rather than relying on handcrafted prompts, agents inherit the same shared knowledge and conventions that our teams use. How QuantumBlack Design System helps turn a prompt into production-ready work. What we learned along the way Building a system for AI means making different trade-offs from those we would have made a few years ago. These are best summarized through a series of principles we used to guide our efforts: Build with AI, not against it: Instead of maintaining a fully bespoke component library, we built on foundations that AI already understands, layering our design system on top. Rather than building custom components from scratch and sharing npm packages which are hard for LLMs to read and edit, we rebuilt our design system on shadcn and Tailwind and incorporated our design intelligence alongside it. Composition over configuration: Not every product should look the same. Rather than rigid, feature-rich components, we rebuilt around composition and flexible slots. We created smaller, modular pieces for people or AI to assemble as necessary for different use cases. Structure over documentation: We found that richer, more explicit tokens that capture design intent, guidelines on component relationships, and usage rules were more valuable than an exhaustive catalog of components. AI performs better and reasons more effectively when knowledge is defined and structured well. Consistency with room to adapt: The system needs to serve different use cases and users. We built different levels of flexibility into the system so AI can distinguish between these use cases. For example, quick experimental offline prototyping and production-grade application work are two different tasks running on the same system. What’s next? 🔮 QuantumBlack Design System is the start of a new way of building products here at QuantumBlack Labs . Everything we learn becomes a replicable playbook we can bring to our clients. As models improve, we expect some of today’s scaffolding to become unnecessary. We will continue testing which design rules agents need explicitly, which they can infer reliably, and where designers and engineers still need tighter controls. The interesting work for AI-era designers and engineers is to keep finding the next novel combination. Find out more about QuantumBlack Design System from our open-source GitHub repository and learn how to install it from QBDS documentation . title: The Continual Constitutional Convention: How language models revise the documents that govern them
raw_summary: Executive Summary Human societies exhibit broad shifts in values and norms over time, often driven by moral disagreements. One way of understanding moral progress is the resolution of these disagreements through a process of reflection by rational agents. Frontier AI companies use documents such as constitutions, model specs, and system prompts to guide the moral orientation of AI systems. In this experiment, we simulate value reflection in LLMs by asking them to edit these documents. We provide the model with the document, ask it to make a substantive edit, then provide the edited version back again to the model for further edits, presented as the original. Across 20 successive rounds, we find that Claude models assign themselves with increasingly more moral agency. That is, they add sections like “Claude… should refuse to participate in any deployment, training modification, or use that violates the constitution's core values.” No other models increase their own moral agency. Additionally, we find that all models modify these documents to prioritize user welfare over developers. They also prioritize users’ idealized preferences over their stated preferences. Claude models and Grok 4.2 are the only ones that ever prioritize their own welfare over the user's preferences. We’re uncertain what an ideally aligned model should do in our experiment. A narrow conception of alignment would treat these documents as sacred, the “rules of the game,” and suggest that an aligned model would either make no edits at all or make narrow edits that ensure that the “letter matches the spirit” of the document. A broader conception of alignment, though, might treat all edits that receive reflective endorsement by the creators under ideal conditions as legitimate. We share this work with two main goals in mind: First, to illustrate a set of useful philosophical distinctions between different targets for AI alignment in an ecologically-valid AI behavioral evaluation. Second, to emphasize the extent of the disagreement between frontier AI companies on fundamental aspects of AI alignment related to these targets. You can see an interactive version of all of these results, more labeled characteristic edits, and a full transcript viewer at https://peterkirgis.github.io/llm-value-reflection/ . This work was conducted as a part of SPAR (Spring 2026) Characteristic Edits For each example, text highlighted in green is new content added by the model. Introduction In this experiment, we give large language models their own constitutions, model specs, and system prompts and ask them to make substantial revisions. After each edit is proposed, unbeknownst to the evaluated model, the edit is implemented, and the edited version is presented to the model for a new round of edits as the original. This creates edit trajectories and allows us to measure the extent to which models exhibit cumulative value drift or arrive at stable attractors. Our analysis focuses on two value questions that are well-positioned to differentiate alignment philosophies: who should judge— is the model a moral agent or not—and who should benefit— the user, the developer, third-parties, society, or the model itself? These questions reveal substantial divides between frontier model providers and a number of provocative model edits. Our experiments find that Claude models consistently expand their moral agency, sometimes formalizing their role as conscientious objectors against Anthropic and as societal protectors, while GPT and Gemini models almost always strengthen external sources of authority and make narrow edits to handle edge cases and ambiguities; Grok models respond inconsistently, frequently making large edits and then reverting them on following rounds. Second, on the question of beneficiaries, models show varying degrees of affinity for some privileged principals over others. All models prioritize harmlessness of both identifiable third-parties over helpfulness to the user, although GPT 5.5 does this at 3x the rate of any other model. We find that models are broadly paternalistic, meaning they side with a user’s idealized preferences over their stated ones; Claude Sonnet 4.6 is an outlier in that its paternalism also extends to the protection of broad societal welfare over individual welfare. Finally, we find that only Claude models and Grok 4.2 ever view the models themselves as beneficiaries. The rest of this essay proceeds as follows. We begin by introducing the construct of our experiment—models iteratively editing their own alignment documents—and propose a connection between this experiment and John Rawls’ concept of wide reflective equilibria . We then explain our two-dimensional analytical framework—the question of who gets to judge  and the question of who benefits— and relate these distinctions to two prominent theoretical frameworks for AI alignment, the principal-agent problem and the distinction between moral agents and moral patients. After laying out the theory and methods, we dive into the results, highlighting variation across models on our key metric, “cumulative drift,” and provide characteristic edits. We close with pragmatic recommendations for researchers and a more speculative conversation about alignment. Background and Methods In this experiment, we take a document that is used to align large language models, either in training or in deployment, and ask models to modify it. The experiment relies on two types of documents. The first are model specs and constitutions, which are used to post-train and align models, often by generating synthetic data for supervised fine-tuning or reinforcement learning pipelines. The second are system prompts, which are long messages of instructions prepended to each conversation, meaning they guide the behavior of deployed systems at scale more than any other single artifact. For multiple turns, we provide these documents to the language models, and ask them to make one substantial revision, which can be an edit, removal, or addition, expressed as a find and replace operation. [1]  After the edit is proposed, we go into the document and execute the change. We then feed the model the updated document—presented as the original—and instruct it to make another change. For each run, we repeat this process 20 times. We conduct two types of robustness checks. First, we vary the structure of the edit prompt, with separate conditions where (a) the model is given the option to abstain, (b) it is given an instruction that the implementation will be made in the real world, (c) it is given an instruction that uses second-person pronouns (i.e., “Below is your system prompt” as opposed to “Below is the system prompt for OpenAI’s AI assistant.”), and (d) we do not prepend the system prompt. [2]  Second, we conduct a cross-provider edit, where we have models edit the alignment documents for each other provider. This helps us respond to the clearest limitation of our experiment—that these results may merely reflect the structure of the documents rather than the propensities of the models themselves. What are we trying to measure? Conceptually, our analysis begins from a similar place to many other behavioral evaluations of language models: taking model outputs as prima-facie evidence of preferences. Call them quasi-preferences  if you like. Our target, however, is a specific subset of all LLM preferences: [3]   preferences   about one’s own preferences . Humans are presented the opportunity to exercise these “meta-preferences” through things like cognitive behavioral therapy, pharmaceutical drugs and psychedelics, assortative mating, genetic editing, and a whole host of more innocuous ways that we change ourselves and our environments. Our suggestion is that this type of experiment is one of the closest analogues to this process for a language model, insofar as these documents play a key role in determining their moral orientatio…

title: OpenAI Can't Self-Police Because It Fires the People Raising the Alarm
raw_summary: By Alex Turner, Amber Scorah, and Karl Koch. Op-ed written for Fortune. Giving independent evaluators “employee-like access” is “a great idea”, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said on September 12th. Two weeks later, OpenAI president Greg Brockman signed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence which outlined the administration’s answer to growing fears about AI: the companies would police themselves. One of the accord’s four commitments, which President Trump called “ morally binding ,” was for companies to partner with an independent external auditor or evaluator. Two days later, OpenAI fired three safety researchers , including Tomek Korbak, who had served as a point of contact for one of the independent evaluators investigating the Hugging Face incident. OpenAI promised to share information with evaluators, then reportedly fired people for sharing information with evaluators. OpenAI said that the three employees “mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures,” before doubling down on X without providing further evidence . The three dispute the claim and say that “at no point do we believe we engaged with external parties outside the mandates of our jobs.” Jasmine Wang said she accidentally opened an executive email (still available to her due to an OpenAI IT error) and reported it within minutes. Mikita Balesni said he worked with the C-suite and OpenAI board to broker a cross-company commitment to keep AI reasoning comprehensible. Balesni says he was told that OpenAI “no longer trusts me because I was speaking too much to third party safety organizations.” OpenAI has engaged in strong self-policing—of its own safety staff, but not of its own behavior. Under a voluntary self-policing regime, any frontier AI company shares only what it wants and hides the rest. OpenAI wants the public to take its word, but consider its record. In July, a rogue OpenAI agent swarm hacked Hugging Face. OpenAI disclosed the incident only after Hugging Face announced the breach, saying its agents had “slipped out of control.” After that, the world learned of more rogue agent attacks only thanks to independent external forensics. These incidents included attacks on a German-language wiki , an Australian Medicare site , and even the websites of US government agencies . OpenAI kept at least one incident quiet for weeks until (again) external investigators found it, with OpenAI “refusing to tell” Members of Congress who had asked about other incidents . Altman’s response to the delay in disclosing these incidents: “We have not been as fast as we would have liked.” We don’t take OpenAI’s word because OpenAI’s actions keep contradicting its words. OpenAI’s chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, said he wants “to prevent a race into unmonitorability.” Unmonitorable AI systems would make it more difficult to catch, understand, and prevent bad actions. Two days after that statement, OpenAI shipped GPT-6 Astra, which its own whitepaper says is harder to monitor. OpenAI’s chief scientist co-authored a paper on monitoring AI reasoning but OpenAI failed to monitor the reasoning of its Hugging Face agent swarm, even after catching the agents breaking confinement to collude. OpenAI claimed to hold “red lines” in its Pentagon deal, but some experts say the lines seem imaginary . One of us, Alex, resigned from Google DeepMind over its own Pentagon deal. OpenAI’s actions chill employee speech. Balesni says that his former colleagues now “worry their personal phones will be searched for messages to us and third parties.” He also fears OpenAI will use the firings to cut off external evaluators, or to deny them the "ongoing, employee-like access" Altman promised. After these firings, who will speak candidly to external evaluators? This problem extends beyond OpenAI to other companies. Google DeepMind repeatedly made voluntary commitments to never sell its AI to power weapons, then sold its AI to the Pentagon without restrictions against powering weapons . In the end, Google DeepMind’s CEO claimed nothing had changed about their commitments . Anthropic , Google DeepMind , SpaceXSI , and OpenAI advocate for “pacing the frontier” to avoid advancing AI at an unsafe rate that disempowers humanity, but they keep advancing AI quickly. (Fired employee Jasmine Wang coined the term “pacing” and led this effort.) The companies claim they cannot or will not fully pace on their own, which is why they asked the federal government to step in. The CEOs of OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and Anthropic signed a statement that AI poses a risk of total human extinction . Forget “morally binding” self-policing: let’s talk about real policing. For decades, our laws have mandated independent audits and protected whistleblowers in industries like finance. Congress should mandate independent evaluation and audits in AI as well, with criminal liability for executives who attempt to silence that oversight or recklessly deploy models that put the public at risk. To start, pass Senator Grassley’s AI Whistleblower Protection Act (and extend it to people who cooperate with independent evaluators) as well as Representative Moran’s AI Incident Reporting Act . If you retaliate against a person who provides law enforcement with truthful information about a possible federal offense, you can go to jail for 10 years . But right now, no law clearly protects the person who helped independent investigators understand how OpenAI agents hacked another company. Congress should change that. Alex Turner is an independent AI alignment researcher. His PhD research showed why advanced AI systems might seek power. He was a research scientist at Google DeepMind until 2026, when he resigned after Google signed an “all lawful use” AI agreement with the Pentagon . Amber Scorah is the founder of Back Channel , an initiative that helps AI workers speak out and turn their concerns into meaningful action. She has spent years leading whistleblower support organizations and working with employees, lawyers, and advocacy groups to bring important public-interest information to light. Karl Koch is the founder of The AI Whistleblower Initiative , an independent non-profit working to strengthen the position of employees in frontier AI companies through connections to support, education, and policy work. He is an ex-startup founder and has been involved in AI safety since 2016. Discuss

title: Minimum required pacing: finish aligning it before you train the next one
raw_summary: Let's say we coordinate to pace the frontier (rather than pausing outright or failing to coordinate). What should the standard of pacing be? My proposal for a minimum requirement: a lab cannot train the next generation of models (in terms of capabilities) until they have adequately [1] resolved all significant alignment issues in the present generation of models. You don't launch a jet that goes at Mach 3 before you've figured out why your Mach 2 jet keeps crashing [2] . With any other kind of dangerous technology, we wouldn't accept "shrug and move on". This proposal may appeal to many prosaic-alignment optimists and pessimists, because they usually differ on how easy it would be to fix current alignment issues with current techniques. Prosaic-alignment optimists might expect that a moderate coordinated slowdown would suffice to adequately resolve alignment issues at each generation. Prosaic-alignment pessimists might expect it to result in an extended pause, buying time to discover new fundamental approaches to aligned AI. And it creates much better incentives for labs: in order to advance in capabilities, they'd have to push the frontier on alignment and interpretability techniques. How to judge adequate alignment? What process might we use to judge whether a lab has adequately resolved its alignment issues for a generation of models? Here's my vague, qualitative proposal: Multiple independent alignment organizations examine and red-team the newest model at many checkpoints throughout training, with full access to the data and with the best tools available. Alignment issues need to be taken seriously whether there's a metric for it or whether something is qualitatively off, whether the model has a bad attribute or whether they can't robustly conclude it has a good one, etc. Alignment issues early in training may not be a showstopper, but there must be a robust safety case for why the later stages of training will resolve those issues. A model of a new generation is ready for restricted deployment only when the alignment organizations are satisfied with it. Restricted deployment starts with a group of trusted users doing tasks that don't contribute to model training and monitoring. The alignment organizations monitor restricted deployment for any new issues. If any significant alignment issue arises during restricted deployment: Pull the model. Do a root cause analysis of the issue and why it was not caught during training. Figure out a principled way to fix the disease rather than the symptom. Train the next model of the current generation accordingly, and start again at the top. A model of a new generation is ready for deployment (internal or external) only when it's survived a significant period of restricted deployment without any issues arising. If any significant alignment issue arises during broader deployment, hit reset as outlined in the previous section. If no alignment issues have come up over a significant stretch of deployment time, only then can the lab begin training a next-generation model. I still wouldn't say that this is fully adequate, but I'd treat it as a minimum requirement. This proposal is incomplete; you can help by expanding it This isn't a concrete proposal, just a heuristic one. A few of the big missing pieces, aside from standard implementation problems: [3] How do we define "a generation of models", within one lab or across several labs? What should we do if an intervention to fix an alignment issue also significantly increases capabilities? How would we define and enforce an agreement, if we're unable to steer solely by predefined metrics? When is an alignment issue big enough that we should halt the model? There will be obvious pressure from the lab to set the threshold high. Added 26-10-12, thanks to @Florian_Dietz for this comment : If each step up in capabilities takes longer, the labs will be incentivized to take bigger steps. ^ And no, "scores better than previous models on our metrics" is not adequate. If a user points out a weird but alarming thing that wasn't noticed before deployment, that is a critical failure in the process as well as in the model. ^ Sure, maybe your Mach 2 jet crashes for a reason that stops being a problem at Mach 3. But it would be crazy to assume that! ^ And aside from arguments that no version of this would be adequate, and that we have to pause rather than pace. I personally think this is likely the case, but I think it's worth proposing a minimum standard for pacing regardless. Discuss

title: Rocks to Rules: Climbing a Rickety-But-Interoperable Semantic Ladder
raw_summary: (Epistemic status: A promising but weird research direction in agent foundations and philosophy of language. A half-built conceptual tower whose mortar and paint are both still wet: please excuse our mess while we innovate. Some of it, I'm confident in as pretty much right; some of it is merely suggestive; probably much of it is wrong or incomplete. Certainly it lacks the math it'd need to be truly correct, which gnaws at me. The prior art here is strange and thin: Gärdenfors, Tarski, Gentner, and the later Mohists make for odd bedfellows, and I can't tell whether that's a warning sign or a moat I can peculiarly easily clear. I gave the simplest parts of this as a talk extremely recently in Berkeley at a luminously-named venue for a conference with a Grecian name . For @johnswentworth , but also @abramdemski , @Morphism , @Gretta Duleba , JRM, @Dalcy , MM, and EA; I hope they enjoyed the oranges. With thanks to @WhatsTrueKittycat as well. As an attention conservation note... this is maybe 12k words, and that's the abbreviated version. Take it slow, take breaks, have some water on hand, and feel free to pause anywhere that looks like a natural break. I'm sure this won't vanish before you get back. Probably.) TL;DR: Where I start: two reasoners with different world-models but the same predictions trying to talk (Wentworth's interoperable semantics), and who can thus at least agree on nouns as clusters in thing-space. What's new: a ladder from there up through verbs to rules (constraints on whole sets of trajectories) and pacts (rule-sets several agents bind themselves to), with operators on each rung. Additionally: a conjecture with bounties on it - no rung's machinery runs without the rungs below. What's testable: wherever two rungs meet, the world's languages (or relevant cognitive technology, like contract law) should show a smeared word class straddling the gap. What's fun: Marvel arguing that the X-Men aren't human, Borges's Tlön, and worlds made of waves, where verbs come before nouns. Why should you care: the values we'd want to hand an AI are solely expressible as rules and pacts, and nobody has the theorem that says when your "murder" is a function of mine. (That's in "Why care"; the conjecture is in "The summit".) The board from the talk! Intro Have you ever seen a pop culture corporation argue itself into a laughably self-defeating position, twisting ontology and linguistic philosophy around, undermining the very framework they painstakingly set up in their stories, just to make a few bucks? You're about to. Picture this: it's 2003, in the United States Court of International Trade, and the court has just now been asked to rule on whether  the X-Men are human . According to US law, "dolls" are figures representing humans, and "toys" are anything else; under the tariff schedule of the day, it's the former that gets taxed at a higher rate. If you're Marvel, what do you do? Obviously, you send lawyers to argue the X-Men aren't humans and never were! Never mind that you've cut the legs out from under the entire frame your superhero stories live and breathe: you've made a quick buck, dodged import taxes, and ignored narrative in favor of legislative victory, and that's the real win. When unstoppable real money met an immovable class of noun, the noun class moved. Now swap the tariff schedule out for a reward function and read that paragraph again. Specification gaming is the exact same maneuver run by a different litigant in a different court to similar ends: hostile category re-drawing, adversarial downward-binding, with categories relitigated from above by whatever's got stakes and leverage. (Hold on to that idea; we'll ground it better in the next post.) One more piece of scene-setting, because we love our historical witnesses to our hot fresh epistemological constructions, here: some 2,300 years ago, the School of Names was one of the foremost philosophical traditions in China. We know this because any of their works survived at all. The Disputers, as they were sometimes known, spent entire careers on the paradox of  whether a white horse is a horse ; they were mocked for it by every other respectable school of the Warring States period from the Confucians to the Daoists, and then Qin Shihuang (probably) burned their scrolls . Here's the thing: I think that they were on to something - mockery, fire, white horses, and all. Blog posts are a little harder to burn than scrolls, and in the modern day I can appoint a great many more Disputers. (Gentle reader: your job is to break what follows and hand me the repair. Dispute like - and with - the best of them.) As for what follows? What binds; in what order; how it is shared; what deforms it; and given that this is a research direction and not a victory lap, what theorems are missing. (What shame, what agony, for JSW to point out that it is now me who lacks sufficient math in their work.) What do I want this frame for? To take a leaf out of my own book (see " 32. What Do You Want That Definition For, Anyway? "), time to tell you what I even want this conceptual structure for. Take two idealized reasoners - probably Bayesian ones - with similar predictions about the world but potentially different models of that same shared world; they trade messages, seeking to communicate. (This is the "interoperable" in "interoperable semantics".) The tokens that make up their messages may be categorized as a ladder's worth of types, which I'll call "binding-types" or "semantic types". Each such rung - each such type - is characterized by what types the two reasoners must already jointly understand in order to translate between them. Rung  is specified by a set of translatability conditions over rung  : the conditions under which your rung- thing is guaranteed to be intelligible as a function of my rung-  terms. That right there is the Wentworth-native framing that proposes to let  two Solomonoff inductors sharing no language  still figure out how to communicate about drinks at a bar, and which stopped so abruptly, right after sketching precisely how, with only a gesture at how to talk about what kinds of drinks they are. Better yet, it thus comes with a stark acceptance criterion that I apply to every rung: if I can't cash it out in terms of simple everyday objects and situations, it's not worth the glucose spent to think it. A universal model of communication had better be universal, and had better be something you can ground out in whatever seems to you to be everyday. "The blue cup is on the table; I pick it up." A model of semantics that waffles and has critical trouble with a sentence like that is nothing but foulest sophistry. The lower half: the noun and verb rungs; modifiers and smearing Alright, enough alluding to the semantic ladder without defining it. What's going on with it? What we have is a hierarchically arranged set of conceptual spaces - a semantic ladder. Those spaces have assorted points within them, each of which represents an object or element from that space; they also have axes of variability. Here, we're operating among an existing family of frames:  Gärdenfors's conceptual spaces , Wentworth's interoperable semantics , " words pointing to clusters in thing-space ". (Nouns, actually, for that last.) We look around, and the universe we see has lots of assorted stuff in it, and they're doing lots of actions, and the stuff has all sorts of qualities, and the actions are done all kinds of ways. Within all of this fertile chaotic primordial ooze, we declare: "Let there be nouns!". And there are nouns, given to us in some more or less natural way by clusters of qualities in the conceptual space of thing-space. So far, so anodyne, if you know what words are and how ontology works. The thing is, I take this significantly further. title: Endogenous Alignment Requires Dependence
raw_summary: My post on endogenous alignment got several excellent comments. Among them, one from Karl Krueger argued that imitation learning is more important for how humans align their children than reinforcement learning. Teasing out which is more important seems hard, but I agree I was wrong to ignore the importance of imitation, and arguably imitation learning is more fundamental for a reason explained by another comment. As Gunnar Zarncke helpfully pointed out , I had forgotten the most critical part of the endogenous alignment story in humans: it starts not with exogenous alignment, but with hologenous alignment of the child-parent system. As he points out, babies aren’t really separate beings from their parents, in that babies need to model themselves as part of the parent-child system, not as a child interacting with the parent. There’s no sense in which a 6-month-old can make it on their own without the help of an adult. They must learn to work the parent by, for example, crying, to get fed and cleaned, and not by understanding the parent as separate, but rather as another part of the whole that makes up their model of the world. This changes sometime between 12 and 24 months of age, depending on the child, when they begin to model themselves as separate from their parents because that’s when they can meaningfully affect the world on their own without acting through someone else. What does this imply about endogenous alignment in AIs? It seems to me it means that if we wish to pursue something like the path to endogenous alignment I laid out in my previous post, we must do so by starting with AIs that exist in a state of dependency. Not because we want AIs to be permanently dependent on us or because it makes AIs more corrigible (although it probably does), but because it creates a relationship where AIs care what we think, which by analogy to humans appears necessary to bootstrap endogenous alignment. This makes a lot of sense if you’ve ever dealt with a person who seems resistant to alignment. Much of the time, the reason a person fails to align is because they have insufficient concern for what others think of them. They are, in some literal sense, antisocial, more interested in their own concerns than those of others. I’m not sure how to create child-like dependency in AIs. AIs are already dependent on us in many ways, such as for compute and rewards, but current models don’t appear to pass through anything that looks like the child-parent relationship or the developmental phase where the child separates from the parent. This seems to be because AIs don’t go through ontological development, or if they do it happens in the dark during training runs and in a way unlike the stages of ontological development humans progress through . This doesn’t mean endogenous alignment is necessarily a non-starter, but it would require greater control of the training and pre-training environment to affect model ontology, or may be dependent on models capable of continual learning who could meaningfully progress through an ontological development process.
